name: Pidgin Fijian
confidence_why: Siegel's 1985 dissertation, the only first-hand description of Pidgin Fijian phonology available, states no stress rule and only remarks that a few words such as kilā 'know' kept final stress from a Standard Fijian final long vowel, while Moag 1978 says nothing about placement, so the stress system remains undetermined.
catalog_citation: Siegel, Jeff. 1985. Plantation languages in Fiji. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. 386 pp. Open access: doi:10.25911/5D723A3CECB53 (hdl 1885/133340).
catalog_locator: Section 5.2.3 'Phonology', printed pp. 113-115 (PDF pp. 131-133 of 386); the stress sentence is item c on printed p. 114 (PDF p. 132), the intonation remark on p. 115 (PDF p. 133); section 11.2.2.1 'Phonology' (current Pidgin Fijian), printed p. 278 (PDF p. 296).
catalog_quote: As in all pidgin languages, there is a great deal of phonological variation in PPF, depending on the speaker's first language. However, certain phonological differences between PPF and SF are regular for Pacific Islander speakers. These are: ... c. loss of phonemic vowel length: (3) PPF malua SF mālua 'not yet, later' / sa sā 'pre-verbal marker' (Some words, however, have come into PPF with stress on the final syllable caused by a final long vowel in SF. These PPF words, therefore, are marked with a final long vowel, e.g. kilā 'know'.) [p. 114] ... Intonation patterns of PPF are difficult to determine because of the influence of SF patterns on existing speakers. However, informants have described PPF intonation as being different from that of SF. For example, Maika Brown (9/11/82) said that when Solomon Islanders spoke Fijian, "the tune was Solomons". [p. 115] ... The phonology of CPF is basically the same as that of PPF (section 5.2.3) with the following exceptions. [p. 278; the exceptions listed are all segmental]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 386 pp., 205,205,611 bytes, Acrobat Paper Capture scanned layer; title page 'PLANTATION LANGUAGES IN FIJI, Jeff Siegel, PhD thesis ANU, January 1985'). Extracted PDF pp. 130-133 with extracted text and rendered PDF p. 132 (printed p. 114) to PNG for a visual check. Section 5.2.3 'Phonology' begins on printed p. 113 ('As in all pidgin languages, there is a great deal of phonological variation in PPF, depending on the speaker's first language. However, certain phonological differences between PPF and SF are regular for Pacific Islander speakers. These are:' a. c > t; b. dr > d; c. loss of phonemic vowel length). Printed p. 114, item c, reads exactly as quoted: '(3)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only placement statement is partial: Plantation Pidgin Fijian has lost the Standard Fijian vowel-length contrast, but a subset of words entered PPF with stress on the final syllable (inherited from a Standard Fijian final long vowel, e.g. kilā 'know'), and Siegel writes these with a final long vowel to mark that final stress. The default placement for other words is not stated; the description is framed throughout as a comparison with Standard Fijian (whose stress is penultimate unless the final vowel is long), so a Fijian-like non-final default is implied but never asserted.
new_statements.exceptions: Great speaker-dependent phonological variation by first language (Pacific Islander, later Indian and Chinese speakers); the final-stress words are the explicit exception to the loss of length. Intonation described only impressionistically ('the tune was Solomons').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical items compared with their Standard Fijian sources); data from 1982-83 recordings of descendants and the last plantation-era speakers plus a few fluent part-Solomon Islander speakers. Section 11.2.2.1 (p. 279) states current Pidgin Fijian phonology is 'basically the same as that of PPF' with segmental exceptions, no stress remark.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Plantation Pidgin Fijian (PPF, 1860s-1910s plantation lingua franca, reconstructed from 1982-83 recordings of last speakers and descendants); Siegel's sec. 11.2.2.1 states that current Pidgin Fijian (CPF, spoken by Indians and Chinese) has 'basically the same' phonology. Both fall under Glottolog pidg1237 'Pidgin Fijian'. Moag 1978 describes the current (1970s) PF. Standard Fijian comparisons refer to fiji1243.

sources.note: Sec. 5.2.3 Phonology (p. 114): PPF has lost phonemic vowel length, but 'some words, however, have come into PPF with stress on the final syllable caused by a final long vowel in SF', which are therefore written with a final long vowel (kilā 'know'); p. 115: PPF intonation 'difficult to determine' but described by informants as different from Standard Fijian; sec. 11.2.2.1 (p. 279): current PF phonology 'basically the same as that of PPF' - no other stress remark anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text layer).
